newsitem.title: UK: Euro products outlook - Follow futures' fortunes.
newsitem.headline: Euro products outlook - Follow futures' fortunes.

text.p: European oil product prices will follow the fortunes of futures which have entered a volatile phase amid the tensions in the Middle East, traders said.
Gas oil remains the key to the market as Europe's citizens dust off their winter wear and start to heat their homes again.
IPE Sept gas oil futures reached post-Gulf War highs at $226.75 a tonne last week, just ahead of the contract's expiry.
The Iraqi crisis showed signs of easing over the weekend but traders continue to monitor the Gulf for clues as to direction.
And gas oil may yet push higher.
Traders said that even without the Iraqi crisis lurking in the background, the market looked strong. Growing heating oil demand, especially out of Germany, was seen as a price prop.
"German demand is picking up. They've been holding back but we could see them buying quite aggressively over the next week which will in turn push prices higher," one trader said.
Other players were more cautious. "If you want to play those sorts of games you would be better off asking your boss for 1,000 marks and going off to the casino," a German trader said.
Low gas oil inventories, partly a hang over from the last fierce winter, back up the product's fundamental strength.
Latest data from the Euroilstock foundation showed middle distillate inventory levels 1.3 percent up on a monthly basis but still a whopping 8.3 percent down from August 1995.

Some dealers had hoped that recent transatlantic arbitrage trade would help quell the flames under IPE gas oil futures prices. At least 80,000 tonnes of gas oil was thought to have been sold to Europe from Canada last week.

But European quality specifications rule out almost all distillate grades produced on the other side of the Atlantic and traders think that even if the numbers theoretically work, few suitable barrels will be found to make the ocean crossing.
Higher up the barrel, however, gasoline may find more support from an arbitrage window working in the other direction.
At least 150,000 tonnes of European gasoline was sold last week to U.S. buyers, who are expected to continue to flirt with refiners in Europe.
Mediterranean markets are better supplied but refinery run cutbacks instigated a couple of weeks ago due to poor margins continue to strip supplies from the market.
European fuel oil's prospects will continue to be closely allied with those of crude. Most traders said sellers were keen to stay long, and were wary of letting product go too cheaply.

The small spread between high and low sulphur fuel -- recently a high sulphur cargo traded at $3 a tonne over a low sulphur cargo -- was expected to widen as the latter continues to build on last week's strength.
Euroilstock data showed fuel oil inventories more than 10 percent down on last year -- with Italy, the main low sulphur buyer, responsible for the lion's share of the stock fall.
Sales of Russian straight-run material into the barge market could strip out a bullish factor from high sulphur prices.
